Disaggregation Modeling in R with INLA: Spatial, Multivariate, and Spatio-Temporal Models

Fernando Rodriguez Avellaneda

King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)
fernando.rodriguezavellaneda@kaust.edu.sa

Paula Moraga

King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)
paula.moraga@kaust.edu.sa

2026-02-02

Abstract

Reliable high-resolution data is often unavailable due to privacy constraints or the high cost of fine-scale sampling, leaving researchers with data aggregated over coarse administrative units. Spatial disaggregation is essential for overcoming this limitation, as it enhances spatial resolution to uncover hidden local patterns and enables policymakers to make more precise, evidence-based decisions. We propose a robust spatial disaggregation framework and extend it to multivariate and spatio-temporal settings. Our approach assumes the existence of an underlying latent Gaussian field that represents the true process at a fine scale; by linking this latent field to the aggregated response variables, we can integrate high-resolution covariates for explanatory purposes. Leveraging the Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA) in R, our models provide a computationally efficient alternative to traditional MCMC methods, allowing for sophisticated uncertainty quantification across complex spatial and temporal dimensions.

1 Introduction

Air pollution is a major public health concern. Recent estimates from the State of Global Air 2025 report suggest that air pollution contributed to 7.9 million deaths worldwide in 2023, highlighting it as one of the leading environmental risk factors for death (Health Effects Institute 2025). In particular, fine particulate matter is one of the clearest examples. Long term exposure to PM2.5 has been consistently associated with increased all cause mortality and with diseases such as respiratory infections, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, ischemic heart disease, lung cancer, and stroke (Cohen et al. 2017; Burnett et al. 2018). In practice, the effects of PM2.5 exposure depend on where people live and move, so identifying local hotspots is important for risk assessment and for targeting interventions (Di et al. 2016).

In many settings, PM2.5 is studied together with other key pollutants, especially PM10 and Ozone. Ozone (O3) has been linked to all cause, cardiovascular, and respiratory mortality (Gryparis et al. 2004; Nuvolone, Petri, and Voller 2018), and particulate matter including PM2.5 and PM10 has shown adverse effects even under short term exposure, contributing to mortality, morbidity, and adverse birth outcomes (Pascal et al. 2014; Lu et al. 2015; Feng et al. 2016). From a practical perspective, this motivates working at a finer spatial scale, since coarse maps can hide localized areas with elevated concentrations (Di et al. 2016). Since these pollutants are often related (at least pairwise), we model them jointly to account for their multivariate spatial structure and to obtain a more coherent set of maps across pollutants, rather than treating each pollutant independently (Qu et al. 2023; Duan et al. 2015).

Aerosols, commonly quantified through Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD), are a key component of atmospheric composition with important implications for both climate and human health (Rap et al. 2013). In particular, AOD at 550 nm is a unitless measure that summarizes how much aerosols in the atmospheric column attenuate light at a reference wavelength in the visible spectrum (Laszlo and Liu 2020). Because AOD provides broad spatial coverage from satellite and reanalysis products, it is often combined with chemical transport models and ground measurements to estimate or forecast surface particulate matter, which makes it useful for air quality monitoring and exposure studies (Donkelaar et al. 2010; Donkelaar, Martin, and Park 2006). Beyond air quality applications, aerosols also influence the Earth’s radiative balance and cloud processes, so AOD is directly connected to climate related impacts and their downstream effects (Boucher et al. 2013; Tai, Val Martin, and Heald 2014).

Despite their importance, many air quality products are only available on coarse spatial or spatio temporal supports, for example CAMS reanalysis products (Inness, Ades, Agustı́-Panareda, et al. 2019; Inness, Ades, Agustí-Panareda, et al. 2019). This can hide local variation and make it difficult to identify small areas with high concentrations. Disaggregation models address this problem by assuming an underlying latent process at a finer scale and linking it to aggregated observations through an aggregation operator, while providing uncertainty quantification and allowing the inclusion of high resolution covariates. In this paper, we focus on a practical R workflow based on the models developed in (Avellaneda, Chacón-Montalván, and Moraga 2026; Avellaneda and Moraga 2025), and we show how to implement spatial, multivariate, and spatio temporal disaggregation with INLA.

We start with a univariate spatial example, where we disaggregate PM2.5 concentrations in Portugal from the coarse CAMS grid to a finer resolution, downscaling from 0.1\(^\circ\) to 0.02\(^\circ\), which corresponds approximately to a change from 10 km to 2 km. We then extend the framework to a multivariate setting using the Linear Model of Coregionalization (LMC), jointly disaggregating PM2.5, PM10, and ozone over Portugal using the same CAMS product (Inness, Ades, Agustı́-Panareda, et al. 2019), targeting the same spatial refinement. Finally, we move to the spatio-temporal setting and disaggregate Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) at 550 nm over India using the EAC4 reanalysis from ECMWF (Inness, Ades, Agustí-Panareda, et al. 2019). In that example, we refine the spatial resolution from \(0.75^\circ\) to \(0.25^\circ\) and the temporal resolution from 3-hourly to hourly, producing spatio-temporal predictions at intermediate time points that are not available in the original product.

Portugal and India were chosen as case studies because they provide clear and realistic settings for disaggregation while keeping the examples computationally manageable. Portugal has a moderate spatial extent, strong coastal influences, and noticeable topographic variation, which makes it a useful region to illustrate how fine scale covariates can help recover local pollution patterns from coarse grids. India provides a larger and more heterogeneous domain, with diverse topography and regions with high aerosol load, making it a relevant example for spatio-temporal disaggregation.

Unlike traditional Bayesian inference methods such as Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), which can be computationally intensive for high-dimensional spatial and spatio-temporal models, our approach relies on the SPDE representation that links Gaussian processes to Gaussian Markov random fields (GMRFs) on a spatial or spatio temporal mesh. This link is important because GMRFs have sparse precision matrices, which makes inference fast and scalable with the integrated nested Laplace approximation implemented in INLA.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we summarize the main disaggregation framework and how it is implemented in R-INLA. We then present three worked examples: Section 3 covers a univariate spatial disaggregation of PM2.5 in Portugal, Section 4 extends the approach to a multivariate model for PM2.5, PM10, and ozone in Portugal, and Section 5 presents a spatio-temporal disaggregation example for AOD at 550 nm in India. We close with a short conclusions section, summarizing practical takeaways and possible extensions.

2 Methodology

In this section, we present the theoretical framework behind our spatial, multivariate, and spatio-temporal disaggregation models. We start with the univariate spatial case, which introduces the main idea of a latent continuous field linked to aggregated observations through an aggregation operator. Building on this setup, we extend the model to the multivariate setting using the Linear Model of Coregionalization (LMC) to jointly represent multiple pollutants. We then return to the univariate formulation and extend it to the spatio-temporal case, where the latent field evolves over space and time. Next, we briefly describe the latent structures used in the spatial and spatio-temporal settings, and we close by outlining how inference is performed with INLA.

2.1 Spatial disaggregation model

Let \(Y_i\) denote the observations in spatial regions \(i=1,\ldots,N\). We assume that underlying these observations there is a continuous latent spatial field that is observed only at an aggregated resolution. This latent continuous model can be expressed as a combination of fixed and random effects as

\[\begin{equation} \begin{aligned} y(\mathbf{s}) &= \boldsymbol{\beta}^\top \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{s}) + z(\mathbf{s}) \\ &= \begin{bmatrix} \beta_0 & \beta_1 & \cdots & \beta_p \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ x_1(\mathbf{s}) \\ \vdots \\ x_p(\mathbf{s}) \end{bmatrix} + z(\mathbf{s}). \end{aligned} \tag{2.1} \end{equation}\]

where \(\beta,X(\mathbf{s})\) represents the \(p\) fixed effects (including the intercept \(\beta_0\)), and \(z(\mathbf{s})\) denotes a spatial Gaussian process.

From the continuous spatial process \(y(\mathbf{s})\), we define an aggregated process over a spatial region \(R \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2\) as

\[\begin{equation} z(R) = \frac{1}{|R|}\int_{R} z(\mathbf{s}),\mathrm{d}\mathbf{s}, \tag{2.2} \end{equation}\]

with \(|R| = \int_{R} \mathrm{d}\mathbf{s}\). We then assume that the observed values arise from the aggregation of the continuous latent process together with a measurement error term. In this case, Equation (2.1) aggregates to the discrete process

\[\begin{equation} y(R_i) = \beta \, X(R_i) + z(R_i) + v_i, \tag{2.3} \end{equation}\]

where \(X(R_i)\) represents the average covariates over the spatial region \(R_i\), \(z(R_i)\) is the aggregated process defined in Equation (2.2), and \(v_i\) is an unstructured noise term, modeled as \(v_i \sim \mathrm{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\epsilon})\).

2.2 Multivariate disaggregation model

Let \(\mathbf{Y}_i = [Y_{i1},\ldots,Y_{iM}]^\top\) denote the multivariate observations available for spatial regions \(R_i\), \(i=1,\ldots,N\). We assume that these areal observations arise from an underlying continuous \(M\)-dimensional latent spatial process \(\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{s})=[y_1(\mathbf{s}),\ldots,y_M(\mathbf{s})]^\top\) observed in the aggregated locations. Following the idas of the univariate spatial case, we represent this latent process using fixed effects and a multivariate spatial random effect, \[\begin{equation} \mathbf{y}(\mathbf{s}) = \mathbf{B}\,\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{s}) + \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{s}), \tag{2.4} \end{equation}\] where \(\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{s})\) collects the covariates (including an intercept) and \(\mathbf{B}\) is the corresponding coefficient matrix.

To model the cross-dependence between variables, we use a Linear Model of Coregionalization (LMC) and write the spatial random effect as \[\begin{equation} \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{s})=\mathbf{\Lambda}\,\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{s}), \tag{2.5} \end{equation}\] where \(\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{s})=[z_1(\mathbf{s}),\ldots,z_M(\mathbf{s})]^\top\) is a vector of independent latent spatial fields and \(\mathbf{\Lambda}\) is an \(M\times M\) matrix that controls the multivariate spatial structure. Under a common identifiability choice, \(\mathbf{\Lambda}\) is taken as lower triangular with ones on the diagonal, so that \[\begin{equation} \begin{bmatrix} w_1(\mathbf{s})\\ w_2(\mathbf{s})\\ \vdots\\ w_M(\mathbf{s}) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0\\ \lambda_{21} & 1 & \cdots & 0\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ \lambda_{M1} & \lambda_{M2} & \cdots & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} z_1(\mathbf{s})\\ z_2(\mathbf{s})\\ \vdots\\ z_M(\mathbf{s}) \end{bmatrix}, \end{equation}\] which implies \[\begin{equation} \begin{aligned} w_1(\mathbf{s}) &= z_1(\mathbf{s}),\\ w_2(\mathbf{s}) &= \lambda_{21}z_1(\mathbf{s}) + z_2(\mathbf{s}),\\ &\ \ \vdots\\ w_M(\mathbf{s}) &= \lambda_{M1}z_1(\mathbf{s}) + \lambda_{M2}z_2(\mathbf{s}) + \cdots + z_M(\mathbf{s}). \end{aligned} \end{equation}\]

To link the continuous model with the areal observations, we use the same aggregation idea as in the univariate case. For a region \(R_i\), we define the aggregated latent quantities as spatial averages, for example \[\begin{equation} \mathbf{z}(R_i)=\frac{1}{|R_i|}\int_{R_i}\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{s})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{s}, \end{equation}\] and we take \(\mathbf{X}(R_i)\) as the covariates averaged over the region \(R_i\). The multivariate observations \(\mathbf{Y}_i\) are then modeled as \[\begin{equation} \mathbf{Y}_i = \mathbf{y}(R_i) = \mathbf{B}\,\mathbf{X}(R_i)+\mathbf{\Lambda}\,\mathbf{z}(R_i)+\mathbf{v}_i, \tag{2.6} \end{equation}\] where \(\mathbf{v}_i=[v_{i1},\ldots,v_{iM}]^\top\) is an unstructured error term at the areal level. A common assumption is independent Gaussian noise by component, \(v_{ij}\sim \mathrm{N}(0,\sigma^2_{v_j})\), for \(j=1,\ldots,M\).

2.3 Spatio-temporal disaggregation model

Based on the univariate spatial formulation, we now include time and treat the data as aggregated over both space and time. Let \(Y_{ij}\) denote the observation for spatial region \(R_i\), \(i=1,\ldots,N\), and time window \(T_j\), \(j=1,\ldots,M\). We assume that these observations come from an underlying continuous spatio-temporal latent process \(y(\mathbf{s},t)\) that we only observe through aggregation over \((R_i,T_j)\). As in the spatial case, we write the latent process as fixed effects plus a structured random effect, \[\begin{equation} y(\mathbf{s},t)=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{s},t) + z(\mathbf{s},t), \tag{2.7} \end{equation}\] where \(\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{s},t)\) represents the fixed effects (including an intercept), and \(z(\mathbf{s},t)\) is a zero-mean spatio-temporal Gaussian process.

To connect the continuous model with the aggregated data, we define the spatio-temporal average of the latent field over a region \(R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\) and a time window \(T\subseteq[0,\infty)\) as \[\begin{equation} z(R,T)=\frac{1}{|R|\,|T|}\int_T\int_R z(\mathbf{s},t)\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{s}\,\mathrm{d}t, \tag{2.8} \end{equation}\] with \(|R|=\int_R \mathrm{d}\mathbf{s}\) and \(|T|=\int_T \mathrm{d}t\). We then assume that the observed values arise from this aggregated latent process plus measurement noise, leading to the discrete model \[\begin{equation} Y_{ij}=y(R_i,T_j)=\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top \mathbf{X}(R_i,T_j) + z(R_i,T_j) + v_{ij}, \tag{2.9} \end{equation}\] where \(\mathbf{X}(R_i,T_j)\) denotes the covariates averaged over region \(R_i\) and time window \(T_j\), and \(v_{ij}\) is an unstructured error term, modeled as \(v_{ij}\sim \mathrm{N}(0,\sigma_{ij}^2)\).

2.4 Spatial structure of the spatial Gaussian process

The spatial random effect \(z(\mathbf{s})\) in the univariate model (Equation (2.2)) and the independent components \(z_j(\mathbf{s})\) in the multivariate model (Equation (2.5)), for \(j=1,\ldots,M\), are modeled as zero-mean Gaussian processes with Matérn spatial dependence (Matérn 1960). Without loss of generality, we describe the structure for a generic field \(\hat{z}(\mathbf{s})\). For two locations \(\mathbf{s}_i\) and \(\mathbf{s}_k\), we assume the Matérn covariance

\[\begin{equation} \text{Cov}(\hat{z}(\mathbf{s}_i), \hat{z}(\mathbf{s}_k)) = \frac{\sigma^{2}}{2^{\nu-1}\Gamma(\nu)} \left(\kappa\left\|\mathbf{s}_i-\mathbf{s}_k\right\|\right)^{\nu} K_{\nu}\left(\kappa\left\|\mathbf{s}_i-\mathbf{s}_k\right\|\right), \end{equation}\]

where \(\sigma^{2}\) is the marginal variance, \(K_{\nu}(\cdot)\) is the modified Bessel function of the second kind, and \(\nu>0\) controls the smoothness of the field. In practice, \(\nu\) is often fixed for stability. The parameter \(\kappa>0\) controls the spatial range, and a common practical definition is \(\rho = \sqrt{8\nu}/\kappa\). This Matérn specification is also convenient for computation, since it has a direct SPDE representation that can be implemented efficiently on a triangulated mesh within the INLA framework.

2.5 Spatio temporal structure of the spatio temporal Gaussian process

In the spatio-temporal disaggregation model, the spatio-temporal Gaussian process \(z(\mathbf{s},t)\) (Equation (2.7)) is specified through the solution of a diffusion-based spatio-temporal SPDE, which directly determines its covariance structure (Lindgren et al. 2023). The construction starts from the spatial operator \(L_s=\gamma_s^2-\Delta\), where \(\gamma_s>0\) and \(\Delta\) is the Laplacian, defined on a domain \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) with suitable boundary conditions. This operator leads to a Whittle Matérn type precision operator \(Q(\gamma_s,\gamma_e,\alpha)=\gamma_e^2 L_s^{\alpha}\). The corresponding spatial field can be written through the SPDE \[\begin{equation} \gamma_e L_s^{\alpha/2}\,\varphi(\mathbf{s}) = \mathcal{W}(\mathbf{s}), \quad \mathbf{s}\in\Omega, \end{equation}\] where \(\mathcal{W}(\mathbf{s})\) denotes spatial white noise. Following the same idea, we define a spatio-temporal noise term \(\mathrm{d}\mathcal{E}_Q(\mathbf{s},t)\) that is temporally uncorrelated but spatially correlated, with precision operator \(Q(\gamma_s,\gamma_e,\alpha_e)\).

Using this noise formulation, we define a spatio-temporal diffusion model with smoothness parameters \((\alpha_t,\alpha_s,\alpha_e)\) and scale parameters \((\gamma_t,\gamma_s,\gamma_e)\): \[\begin{equation} \left(\gamma_t \frac{d}{dt} + L_s^{\alpha_s} \right)^{\alpha_t} v(\mathbf{s}, t) = \mathrm{d} \mathcal{E}_Q(\mathbf{s}, t), \quad (\mathbf{s}, t) \in \Omega \times \mathbb{R}. \tag{2.10} \end{equation}\] The solution \(v(\mathbf{s},t)\) defines a Gaussian process. In this parameterization, \(\alpha_e\) controls the degree of separability, and \(\alpha_e=0\) yields a fully nonseparable model. A convenient summary of this behavior is the nonseparability index \[\begin{equation} \beta_s = 1 - \frac{\alpha_e}{\alpha} = 1 - \frac{\alpha_e}{\nu_s + d/2}, \end{equation}\] where \(\nu_s\) denotes the smoothness of the spatial process and \(\beta_s\in[0,1]\), with \(\beta_s=0\) corresponding to a separable model and \(\beta_s=1\) to a fully nonseparable model (Lindgren et al. 2023). In this paper, we use the nonseparable first-order diffusion model with \((\alpha_t,\alpha_s,\alpha_e)=(1,2,1)\), which corresponds to the \(\texttt{model = "121"}\) specification in INLAspacetime.

For the univariate spatial model in Section 2.1 and the multivariate spatial model in Section 2.2, inference is performed using the SPDE approach implemented in INLA. The main idea is that each latent spatial Gaussian process, either \(z(\mathbf{s})\) in the univariate case or \(z_j(\mathbf{s})\) for \(j=1,\ldots,M\) in the multivariate case, can be represented as the solution of a Mat'ern SPDE (Whittle 1963). Since the same construction applies to each latent field, without loss of generality we describe it for a generic field \(\hat{z}(\mathbf{s})\).

A Mat'ern Gaussian random field can be characterized through the SPDE \[\begin{equation} \left(\kappa^2-\Delta\right)^{\alpha / 2}\big(\tau\,\hat{z}(\mathbf{s})\big)=\vartheta(\mathbf{s}), \tag{2.11} \end{equation}\] where \(\vartheta(\mathbf{s})\) is spatial white noise, \(\alpha\) controls smoothness (with \(\nu=\alpha-d/2\) in dimension \(d\)), and \((\kappa,\tau)\) control the range and marginal variance of the field. The SPDE representation is convenient because INLA approximates \(\hat{z}(\mathbf{s})\) on a triangulated mesh, leading to a Gaussian Markov random field with a sparse precision matrix and fast inference (Rue, Martino, and Chopin 2009).

Let \(\{\mathbf{s}^*_k\}_{k=1}^G\) be the mesh vertices and \(\{\psi_k(\mathbf{s})\}\) the associated piecewise linear basis functions. The latent field is approximated by \[\begin{equation} \hat{z}(\mathbf{s}) \approx \sum_{k=1}^{G}\psi_k(\mathbf{s})\,\hat{z}_k, \tag{2.12} \end{equation}\] where \(\hat{z}_k\) are Gaussian weights defined on the mesh nodes. In disaggregation models we do not observe \(\hat{z}(\mathbf{s})\) directly. Instead, the data are available as spatial averages over regions \(R_i\). Following (Moraga et al. 2017), the key step is to link the areal quantity \(\hat{z}(R_i)=\frac{1}{|R_i|}\int_{R_i}\hat{z}(\mathbf{s})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{s}\) to the mesh representation. Substituting Equation (2.12) into this average gives the core approximation \[\begin{align} \begin{split} \hat{z}(R_i) &= \frac{1}{|R_i|}\int_{R_i} \hat{z}(\mathbf{s})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{s} = \frac{1}{|R_i|}\int_{R_i} \sum_{k=1}^{G} \psi_k(\mathbf{s})\,\hat{z}_k \,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{s} \\ &= \frac{1}{|R_i|}\sum_{k=1}^{G}\left(\int_{R_i} \psi_k(\mathbf{s})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{s}\right)\hat{z}_k \\ &\approx \frac{1}{|R_i|}\sum_{k=1}^{G}\left(\int_{R_i} \psi_k(\mathbf{s}^*_k)\,1_{\{\psi_k(\mathbf{s})\neq 0\}}\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{s}\right)\hat{z}_k \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^{G}\frac{|R_{ik}|}{|R_i|}\,\hat{z}_k = \sum_{k=1}^{G} A_{ik}\,\hat{z}_k, \qquad \text{with}\qquad A_{ik}=\frac{|R_{ik}|}{|R_i|}. \end{split} \tag{2.13} \end{align}\] The matrix \(\mathbf{A}=(A_{ik})\) is the projection (aggregation) matrix that maps the latent field from the mesh nodes to the areal supports. By construction, \(A_{ik}\ge 0\) and each row sums to one, \(\sum_k A_{ik}=1\). In practice, when the mesh is close to regular, we often use the simplified choice \(A_{ik}=1/n_i\) for the \(n_i\) mesh nodes that fall inside region \(R_i\).

This construction is the same for the univariate and multivariate spatial models. In the univariate case, \(\mathbf{A}\) links the latent field to the areal observations in Equation (2.3). In the multivariate case, the same projection idea is applied to each independent component \(z_j(\mathbf{s})\), \(j=1,\ldots,M\), and the LMC structure is then obtained by combining these projected components according to Equation (2.5). In INLA, these mappings are implemented by defining the SPDE model on the mesh and supplying the projection matrices in the inla.stack() objects for estimation and prediction.

3 Spatial disaggregation of PM2.5 concentration in Portugal

In this section, we illustrate spatial disaggregation by improving the resolution of PM2.5 concentrations in Portugal from 10km to 2km. We used annual air quality reanalysis data for Portugal provided by the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) (Inness, Ades, Agustı́-Panareda, et al. 2019), a high-resolution product developed by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). This publicly accessible dataset, available at https://ads.atmosphere.copernicus.eu/datasets/cams-europe-air-quality-reanalyses, integrates satellite observations and auxiliary information to get estimations of air pollution levels in a very corase resolution.

3.1 Data acquisition and preprocessing

To download the data, you need to create an account on the Atmospheric Data Store (ADS), accept the terms and conditions, and obtain the “Licence to use Copernicus Products.” After setup, the data can be downloaded using the Python API. More details on setting up the API are available at https://ads.atmosphere.copernicus.eu/how-to-api. In our request, the argument \(\texttt{variable = ["particulate_matter_2.5um"]}\) selects PM2.5 concentrations, \(\texttt{model = ["ensemble"]}\) specifies the ensemble product, \(\texttt{level = ["0"]}\) indicates the surface level, \(\texttt{type = ["validated_reanalysis"]}\) requests the validated reanalysis product, and \(\texttt{year = ["2019"]}\) and \(\texttt{month = ["01"]}\) restrict the download to January 2019.

After downloading and unzipping the data, we use the terra package to read the \(\texttt{nc}\) file. NetCDF (Network Common Data Form) files are widely used for storing multi-dimensional scientific data, such as climate or GIS datasets, because they are self-describing, portable, and efficient for large arrays. The original dataset contains hourly samples for the 31 days of January 2019, totaling 744 observations. Since our focus is on identifying mean trends, we calculated the average PM2.5 concentration for each location. As the original data covers the entire European continent, we cropped the spatial extent to focus specifically on Portugal. To provide better geographical context in our visualizations, we also included the administrative boundaries of Portugal and Spain for clear regional identification using packages rnaturalearth and sf. Finally for plotting we used ggplot2, tidyterra and viridis packages.

To simplify replication and avoid the ADS download and NetCDF preprocessing steps, we provide the preprocessed dataset as \(\texttt{pm2p5_portugal.csv}\), which contains the processed PM2.5 values in CSV format.

# Define the squared study region and convert to dataframe
sq <- ext(-9.65, -6.05, 36.85, 42.25)


# Read the dataset and compute mean value (From source)
r <- rast("data/cams.eaq.vra.ENSa.pm2p5.l0.2019-01.nc")
r_mean <- app(r, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
r_sq <- crop(r_mean, sq)
df <- as.data.frame(r_sq, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)
df <- df[order(df$y,df$x), ]
names(df) <- c("longitude","latitude","pm2p5")
write.csv(df, "data/pm2p5_portugal.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# Read dataset from preprocess file
df <- read.csv("data/pm2p5_portugal.csv")

# Get portugal and Spain borders
boundary <- ne_countries(scale="medium", returnclass="sf") |>
  subset(admin %in% c("Portugal","Spain")) |>
  st_transform(4326)

# Plot PM2.5 contamination and boundary countries
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = r_sq) +
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "black") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "PM2.5") +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9)
  ) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(xmin(sq), xmax(sq)),
           ylim = c(ymin(sq), ymax(sq)),
           expand = FALSE)

Figure 3.1: Mean PM2.5 concentration in Portugal during January 2019. Country boundaries for Portugal and Spain are overlaid for geographic reference.

Figure (3.1) shows the spatial distribution of mean PM2.5 over the Portugal for January 2019. Higher concentrations are observed in northern Portugal. The map is provided on the original CAMS grid (about 0.1\(^\circ\), roughly 10 km), which is relatively coarse for local-scale interpretation; we therefore target a finer resolution of 0.02\(^\circ\) (approximately 2 km) using spatial disaggregation.

3.2 Input grid, spatial mesh, and prediction locations

The first step in the disaggregation workflow is to construct an input grid that matches the support of the observed data. Using the dataframe \(\texttt{df}\), we build a squared grid as an \(\texttt{sf}\) object with the same spatial extent and dimensions as the original dataset. The second step is to build a spatial mesh that is finer than the initial resolution of the data, as shown on the right side of Figure (3.2). This panel displays a portion of the triangulated mesh, represented by black segments, together with the original gridded support, shown in red. Finally, to achieve the target disaggregation from 0.1\(^\circ\) to 0.02\(^\circ\), we define the prediction points on the desired high resolution grid. The variable \(\texttt{spf}\) controls the disaggregation factor. Specifically, setting \(\texttt{spf}=5\) increases the resolution within each original cell by a factor of \(5 \times 5 = 25\), as illustrated on the left side of Figure (3.2), where red lines denote the original grid and blue dots indicate the prediction locations under the disaggregated scenario.

# Initial squared grid
map <- st_as_sf(st_make_grid(sq, n = c(length(unique(df$longitude)),
                               length(unique(df$latitude)))))
st_geometry(map) <- "geometry"
st_crs(map) <- "EPSG:4326"

# Spatial mesh

sq_sf <- st_as_sf(as.polygons(sq))

hexpts <- fm_hexagon_lattice(
  bnd = st_buffer(sq_sf, 0.1),
  edge_len = 0.05
)

mesh <- fm_mesh_2d(
  loc = hexpts,
  max.edge = 0.1,
  offset = 0.05
)

# prediction points

spf <- 5 # spatial factor
def <- abs(unique(df$latitude)[2]-unique(df$latitude)[1])/2

x <- seq(min(df$longitude) - def*((spf-1)/spf),
         max(df$longitude) + def*((spf-1)/spf),
         length.out = length(unique(df$longitude))*spf)

y <- seq(min(df$latitude) - def*((spf-1)/spf),
         max(df$latitude) + def*((spf-1)/spf),
         length.out = length(unique(df$latitude))*spf)

dp <- as.matrix(expand.grid(x, y))
dpdf <- data.frame(dp)
names(dpdf) <- c("x","y")

dpdf_sf <- st_as_sf(dpdf,coords = c("x","y"),crs="EPSG:4326")
dpdf_sf$id <- 1:nrow(dpdf)

# Plots
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), pty = "s")
plot(mesh,xlim = c(-9.65,-9.45),ylim = c(36.5,37.5))
plot(map$geometry, add = TRUE, border = "red", lwd = 2)

plot(map$geometry, border = "red", lwd = 2 ,xlim = c(-9.7,-9.5),ylim = c(36.8,37))
plot(dpdf_sf$geometry, add = TRUE, col = "blue", lwd = 1)

Figure 3.2: Spatial discretization for disaggregation. Original grid support is shown in red. Prediction points for $ exttt{spf}=5$ are shown in blue (left), and a portion of the triangulated mesh is shown in black (right)

3.3 Covariates

We incorporate high resolution elevation data, at approximately \(60\)m resolution, from the EuroDEM product maintained by EuroGeographics (EuroGeographics and European NMCAs 2023) that is available in the following website https://www.mapsforeurope.org/datasets/euro-dem. Elevation is included as a covariate to relate PM2.5 concentrations with changes in altitude and to improve the explanatory power of the spatial disaggregation model across the study region. To use this covariate within the disaggregation framework, we align its spatial support with both the original CAMS grid and the high resolution prediction grid, by aggregating elevation to the 0.1\(^\circ\) input cells and extracting values at the 0.02\(^\circ\) prediction locations. Figure (3.3) illustrates the resulting elevation focused on Portugal, on the input grid, shown on the left, and at the prediction points, shown on the right. This step can be computationally demanding because EuroDEM is provided at very fine resolution and covers all of Europe, and it must be reprojected to EPSG:4326 before cropping. To reduce computation time, we provide a preprocessed version already reprojected, aggregated and cropped to the study region called \(\texttt{eurodemc.tif}\).

# Time consuming: This preprocessing takes roughly 40 minutes to be executed
# r <- rast("data/eurodem.tif")
# r_map <- project(r, "EPSG:4326")
# writeRaster(r_map, "data/eurodemp.tif", overwrite = TRUE)
# r_map <- rast("data/eurodemp.tif")
# r_crop <- crop(r_map,sq_sf)
# r_ag <- aggregate(r_crop, fact = 2, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
# writeRaster(r_ag, "data/eurodemc.tif", overwrite = TRUE)

# Time consuming: after preprocessing this part takes around 1 minute to be executed
r_crop <- rast("data/eurodemc.tif")
r_crop[is.na(r_crop)] <- 0

# Extract elevation values in the original dataset
map$elev <- terra::extract(r_crop,map,mean)$eurodem

# Create the prediction dataset in sf format
map_pred <- st_as_sf(st_make_grid(sq, n = c(length(unique(df$longitude)),
                               length(unique(df$latitude)))*spf))
st_crs(map_pred) <- "EPSG:4326"

# Extract elevation values in the prediction dataset
map_pred$elev <- terra::extract(r_crop,map_pred,mean)$eurodem

# Plot elevation in the input grid
p1 <- ggplot(map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = elev), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Elevation (m)") +
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "black") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-10, -6), ylim = c(36.5,42.5),
           expand = FALSE) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 5.5, r = 5.5, b = 18, l = 5.5)
  )

# Plot elevation in the prediction grid
p2 <- ggplot(map_pred) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = elev), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Elevation (m)") +
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "black") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-10, -6), ylim = c(36.5,42.5),
           expand = FALSE) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 5.5, r = 5.5, b = 18, l = 5.5)
  )

p1 + p2

Figure 3.3: Elevation over Portugal on the input grid (left) and the prediction grid (right), with country boundaries for reference.

3.4 Model

The main objective of this model is to perform spatial disaggregation by increasing the resolution from 0.1\(^\circ\) to 0.02\(^\circ\), which corresponds approximately to a change from 10 km to 2 km using INLA . We assume the existence of a latent continuous spatial process for PM2.5 that is only observed through aggregated measurements, and it is linked to the observations through the aggregation operator in Equation (??). The latent PM2.5 field is then defined as

\[\begin{equation} \text{pm}_{2.5}(\mathbf{s}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{elevation}(\mathbf{s}) + z(\mathbf{s}) + e(\mathbf{s}) \tag{3.1} \end{equation}\]

where \(\beta_0\) is an intercept and \(\beta_1\) is the regression coefficient associated with elevation. The term \(z(\mathbf{s})\) represents a spatially structured random effect, modeled as a zero mean Gaussian process with a Matérn covariance function, and \(e(\mathbf{s})\) is an unstructured error term, modeled as a zero mean Gaussian process that is independent across space.

3.5 Model inputs for INLA

To fit the model described in Equation (3.1), we use the triangulated mesh defined before in Section 3.2. We then construct the SPDE representation on this mesh, and build the corresponding projection matrices that link the observation locations and the prediction points to the mesh nodes. Finally, we combine the response, covariates, and latent components into stacks, which are used to perform model estimation and prediction.

# Construct the SPDE in the spatial mesh
spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh, alpha = 2, constr = TRUE)

n.ar <- nrow(map) # number of initial regions
nv <- mesh$n # number of mesh nodes

mesh_sf <- st_as_sf(data.frame(x=mesh$loc[,1],y=mesh$loc[,2],id=1:nv),
                    coords = c("x","y"),crs="EPSG:4326")

# Projection matrix from initial data to the triangulated mesh
A.m <- matrix(0, n.ar, nv)
inter <- as.list(st_contains(map[,c()],mesh_sf))

for (i in 1:n.ar){
  idx <- inter[[i]]
  A.m[i,idx] <- 1/length(idx)
}
A.m <- as(A.m, "dgCMatrix")

# Projection matrix from the mesh to the predicted points
A.pr <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = dp)

# Stack for estimation
stk.est <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = df$pm2p5),
  A = list(A.m,A.m,1),
  effects = list(
    s = 1:nv,
    b0 = rep(1, nv),
    elev = map$elev/1000 # convert m to km
  ),
  tag = "y")

# Stack for prediction
stk.pred <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = NA),
  A = list(A.pr,A.pr,1),
  effects = list(
    s = 1:nv,
    b0 = rep(1, nv),
    elev = map_pred$elev/1000 # convert m to km
    ),
  tag = "y.pred")

# Stack for estimation and prediction
stk.full <- inla.stack(stk.est, stk.pred)

3.6 Fitting the model with INLA

Now, we translate Equation (3.1) into an \(\texttt{INLA}\) formula, where the symbol \(\texttt{~}\) defines the linear predictor for the response \(y\). The term \(\texttt{0 + b0}\) adds an explicit intercept, with \(\texttt{b0}\) being a column of ones included in the stack. The term \(\texttt{elev}\) represents elevation as a fixed effect, and \(\texttt{f(s, model = spde)}\) specifies the spatial random effect on the mesh using the SPDE model. We fit the model with \(\texttt{inla()}\) using the stacked data object \(\texttt{stk.full}\), and set \(\texttt{family = "gaussian"}\) because \(y\) is continuous. If the response \(y\) is non Gaussian, such as counts modeled with a Poisson variable, the model specification need to be adapted. For these settings, we recomend using the package inlabru along INLA that provides a workflow to deal with that kind of data (Bachl et al. 2019).

# Time consuming: This preprocessing takes roughly 5 minutes to be executed

# INLA formula
form <- y ~ 0 + b0 + elev + f(s, model = spde)

# Fitting and prediction
res <- inla(
  formula=form,
  #verbose = TRUE,
  data = inla.stack.data(stk.full, spde = spde),
  family = "gaussian",
  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stk.full),
                           compute = TRUE, link = 1)
)

# Summary for the fixed effects
res$summary.fixed |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Table 3.1: Table 3.2: Posterior summary of the fixed effects (intercept and elevation coefficient) for the PM2.5 concentration model in Portugal.
mean sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant mode kld
b0 8.345 0.022 8.303 8.345 8.387 8.345 0
elev -0.439 0.073 -0.582 -0.439 -0.297 -0.439 0

Table (3.1) summarizes the posterior distributions of the fixed effects. The posterior mean of the intercept \(\beta_0\) is 8.29~\(\mu\)g/m\(^3\), which represents the mean PM2.5 level over Portugal when elevation is zero. The posterior credible interval for the elevation coefficient excludes zero, indicating a clear association between elevation and PM2.5. The posterior mean is \(-0.24\), implying that an increase of 1~km in altitude is associated with a decrease of about 0.24~\(\mu\)g/m\(^3\) in PM2.5.

3.7 Input data and predicted values

Figure (3.4) compares the coarse input PM2.5 field (left) with the posterior mean predictions from the disaggregation model on the finer grid (right). The disaggregated surface provides a smoother and more detailed representation of spatial variability, while maintaining the main concentration levels and spatial patterns observed in the input data.We also notice that the range of the predicted surface is slightly wider than the range of the input data. This is an important advantage of the disaggregation approach, since it can reveal localized areas with higher or lower concentrations than suggested by the coarse grid, which can be useful for decision makers.

# get indexes of the response variable
idx <- inla.stack.index(stk.full, 'y.pred')$data

# Input grid
map$pm2p5 <- df$pm2p5

# Prediction
map_pred$pm2p5 <- res$summary.linear.predictor[idx, "mean"]

# Plot for input grid
p1 <- ggplot(map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = pm2p5), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Pm2.5") +
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "black") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-10, -6), ylim = c(36.5,42.5),
           expand = FALSE) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 5.5, r = 5.5, b = 18, l = 5.5)
  )

# Plot for predictions
p2 <- ggplot(map_pred) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = pm2p5), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Pm2.5") +
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "black") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-10, -6), ylim = c(36.5,42.5),
           expand = FALSE) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 5.5, r = 5.5, b = 18, l = 5.5)
  )

# Combine plots
p1 + p2

Figure 3.4: PM2.5 over Portugal on the input grid (left) and disaggregated predictions on the finer grid (right).

4 Multivariate Spatial disaggregation of PM2.5, PM10 and Ozone concentrations in Portugal.

In this section, we extend the previous spatial disaggregation framework to a multivariate setting, jointly modeling PM2.5, PM10, and ozone concentrations in Portugal while increasing the spatial resolution from approximately 10 km to 2 km. We use the same CAMS air quality reanalysis data described in Section 3, now incorporating the additional PM10 and ozone fields. The main difference with respect to the univariate case is that the three pollutants are modeled simultaneously, which allows the model to account for their cross dependence and to borrow strength across variables, improving prediction accuracy.

4.1 Data acquisition and preprocessing

To download the data, we follow the same procedure described in Section 3.1. If the code for the univariate spatial example has already been run, there is no need to repeat the registration or licence acceptance steps. The API request remains the same, except that the \(\texttt{variable}\) argument must now include the three pollutants of interest. Specifically, to download PM2.5 PM10, and ozone concentrations for January 2019, we replace the univariate specification with

\[ \texttt{"variable" = ["particulate_matter_2.5um", "particulate_matter_10um", "ozone"]}. \]

All other request arguments are kept unchanged from the univariate case described in Section 3.1. After downloading and unzipping the data, we follow the same preprocessing steps described in Section 3.1. In this case, we have download three \(\texttt{nc}\) files and for each file we applied a cleaning process, of grouping the observation in space by the mean and then restricting the area of observation to Portugal. To keep the workflow easy to reproduce, and following the univariate example, we also provide the resulting preprocessed data as \(\texttt{mult-data.csv}\), which contains the processed PM2.5, PM10, and ozone values in CSV format.

# Define the squared study region and convert to dataframe
sq <- ext(-9.65, -6.05, 36.85, 42.25)

# Read the dataset,compute mean value and crop pm2.5 (From source)
r_pm2p5 <- rast("data/cams.eaq.vra.ENSa.pm2p5.l0.2019-01.nc")
r_mean_pm2p5 <- app(r_pm2p5, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
r_sq_pm2p5 <- crop(r_mean_pm2p5, sq)

# Read the dataset, compute mean value and crop pm10 (From source)
r_pm10 <- rast("data/cams.eaq.vra.ENSa.pm10.l0.2019-01.nc")
r_mean_pm10 <- app(r_pm10, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
r_sq_pm10 <- crop(r_mean_pm10, sq)

# Read the dataset, compute mean and crop Ozone (From source)
r_o3 <- rast("data/cams.eaq.vra.ENSa.o3.l0.2019-01.nc")
r_mean_o3 <- app(r_o3, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
r_sq_o3 <- crop(r_mean_o3, sq)

# Clean and standardize the data frame
pm2p5 <- as.data.frame(r_sq_pm2p5, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)
pm10 <- as.data.frame(r_sq_pm10, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)
o3 <- as.data.frame(r_sq_o3, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)

# Clean and standardize the data frame
pm2p5 <- as.data.frame(r_sq_pm2p5, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)
pm10 <- as.data.frame(r_sq_pm10, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)
o3 <- as.data.frame(r_sq_o3, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)

# Merge and organize information
dfm <- Reduce(function(x, y) merge(x, y, by = c("x", "y")), list(pm2p5, pm10, o3))
dfm <- dfm[order(dfm$y,dfm$x), ]
names(dfm) <- c("longitude","latitude","pm2p5","pm10","ozone")
write.csv(dfm, "data/mult-data.csv", row.names = FALSE)

Figure (4.1) displays the spatial distribution of mean PM2.5, PM10, and ozone over Portugal for January 2019 on the original CAMS grid (about 0.1\(^\circ\), roughly 10 km), which is relatively coarse for local-scale interpretation. The maps suggest a positive spatial association between PM2.5 and PM10, with areas of higher PM2.5 generally aligning with higher PM10. In contrast, ozone shows an opposite spatial pattern, indicating a negative spatial association with PM2.5 and PM10, where higher particulate concentrations tend to coincide with lower ozone levels.

# Read dataset from preprocess file
dfm <- read.csv("data/mult-data.csv")

# Save it as rast files for plotting
r_sq_pm2p5 <- rast(dfm[,c("longitude","latitude","pm2p5")])
r_sq_pm10 <- rast(dfm[,c("longitude","latitude","pm10")])
r_sq_o3 <- rast(dfm[,c("longitude","latitude","ozone")])

# Get portugal and Spain borders
boundary <- ne_countries(scale="medium", returnclass="sf") |>
  subset(admin %in% c("Portugal","Spain")) |>
  st_transform(4326)

# Plot PM2.5 contamination and boundary countries
p1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = r_sq_pm2p5) +
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "black") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "PM2.5") +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9)
  ) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(xmin(sq), xmax(sq)),
           ylim = c(ymin(sq), ymax(sq)),
           expand = FALSE)

# Plot PM10 contamination and boundary countries
p2 <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = r_sq_pm10) +
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "black") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "PM10") +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9)
  ) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(xmin(sq), xmax(sq)),
           ylim = c(ymin(sq), ymax(sq)),
           expand = FALSE)

# Plot Ozone contamination and boundary countries
p3 <- ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = r_sq_o3) +
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "black") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Ozone") +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9)
  ) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(xmin(sq), xmax(sq)),
           ylim = c(ymin(sq), ymax(sq)),
           expand = FALSE)

p1+p2+p3

Figure 4.1: Mean PM2.5, PM10 and Ozone concentration in Portugal during January 2019. Country boundaries for Portugal and Spain are overlaid for geographic reference.

4.2 Input grid, spatial mesh, and prediction locations

In this section, we replicate the procedure described in 3.2 for the multivariate dataset \(\texttt{dfm}\). Since the steps depend only on the spatial dimensions of the data, we can reuse the same code to construct the input grid, the spatial mesh, and the prediction locations, as in 3.2. The result spatial mesh, input grid and prediction data result of this step have to looks like in the Figure (3.2).

# Initial squared grid
map <- st_as_sf(st_make_grid(sq, n = c(length(unique(dfm$longitude)),
                               length(unique(dfm$latitude)))))
st_geometry(map) <- "geometry"
st_crs(map) <- "EPSG:4326"

# Spatial mesh

# convert the square in a sf object
sq_sf <- st_as_sf(as.polygons(sq))

# Create equally space points for the emsh
hexpts <- fm_hexagon_lattice(
  bnd = st_buffer(sq_sf, 0.1),
  edge_len = 0.05
)

# Create the mesh based in the previous points
mesh <- fm_mesh_2d(
  loc = hexpts,
  max.edge = 0.1,
  offset = 0.05
)

# mesh as a sf object
mesh_sf <- st_as_sf(data.frame(x=mesh$loc[,1],y=mesh$loc[,2],id=1:mesh$n),
                    coords = c("x","y"),crs="EPSG:4326")

# prediction points
spf <- 5 # spatial factor
def <- abs(unique(dfm$latitude)[2]-unique(dfm$latitude)[1])/2

x <- seq(min(dfm$longitude) - def*((spf-1)/spf),
         max(dfm$longitude) + def*((spf-1)/spf),
         length.out = length(unique(dfm$longitude))*spf)

y <- seq(min(dfm$latitude) - def*((spf-1)/spf),
         max(dfm$latitude) + def*((spf-1)/spf),
         length.out = length(unique(dfm$latitude))*spf)

dp <- as.matrix(expand.grid(x, y))
dpdfm <- data.frame(dp)
names(dpdfm) <- c("x","y")

dpdfm_sf <- st_as_sf(dpdfm,coords = c("x","y"),crs="EPSG:4326")
dpdfm_sf$id <- 1:nrow(dpdfm)

4.3 Covariates

As in Section 3.3, we use elevation from the EuroDEM product (EuroGeographics and European NMCAs 2023) as a high resolution covariate, and we align its support with both the 0.1\(^\circ\) CAMS input grid and the 0.02\(^\circ\) prediction grid. In the multivariate setting, elevation is included to explain shared altitude related variability across PM2.5, PM10, and ozone, and to improve the explanatory power of the joint disaggregation model over Portugal. For reproducibility and to reduce computation time, we use the same preprocessed raster \(\texttt{eurodemc.tif}\) described in the univariate case, which is already reprojected to EPSG:4326, aggregated, and cropped to the study region. Therefore, if the univariate example has already been run, this preprocessing step does not need to be repeated.

# Time consuming: after preprocessing this part takes around 1 minute to be executed
r_crop <- rast("data/eurodemc.tif")
r_crop[is.na(r_crop)] <- 0

# Extract elevation values in the original dataset
map$elev <- terra::extract(r_crop,map,mean)$eurodem

# Create the prediction dataset in sf format
map_pred <- st_as_sf(st_make_grid(sq, n = c(length(unique(dfm$longitude)),
                               length(unique(dfm$latitude)))*spf))
st_crs(map_pred) <- "EPSG:4326"

# Extract elevation values in the prediction dataset
map_pred$elev <- terra::extract(r_crop,map_pred,mean)$eurodem

4.4 Model

The multivariate disaggregation model, uses the relation between response variable and the information of fine resolution covariates. This model, as the univariate case, assumes the existence of three independent latent continuous spatial process to express the response variable as a linear combination of this processes using the Linear Model of Corregionalization (LMC). Then for a \(M\)-multivariate response variable \(\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{s}) = [W_1(\mathbf{s}), \dots, W_M(\mathbf{s})]^\top\), we can express this using the LCM as \(\mathbf{W}(\textbf{s}) = \mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{{U}}(\textbf{s})\) where \(\{\mathbf{U}(\textbf{s})\}\) represents \(M\) independent latent spatial processes and \(\Lambda\) is a \(M\) dimensional squared matrix that defined the multivariate correlation structure between response variables.

For identifiability of the independent processes \(\mathbf{U}(\mathbf{s})\), constraints must be imposed on the coregionalization matrix \(\mathbf{\Lambda}\) to avoid rotational aliasing, requiring \(M \times (M-1)\) restrictions. A common choice is to set \(\mathbf{\Lambda}\) as a lower triangular matrix with ones on the diagonal (Geweke and Zhou 1996). Under these conditions the response variable \(\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{s})\) could be expresed as

\[\begin{equation*} \begin{bmatrix} W_1(\textbf{s}) \\ W_2(\textbf{s}) \\ \vdots \\ W_M(\textbf{s}) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ \lambda_{21} & 1& \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \lambda_{M1} & \lambda_{M2} & \cdots & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} U_1(\textbf{s}) \\ U_2(\textbf{s}) \\ \vdots \\ U_M(\textbf{s}) \end{bmatrix} \tag{4.1} \end{equation*}\]

This leads to the following system of equations:

\[\begin{align} \begin{split} W_1(\textbf{s}) & = U_1(\textbf{s}), \\[3mm] W_2(\textbf{s}) & = \lambda_{21} U_1 (\textbf{s}) + U_2(\textbf{s}), \\[3mm] & \hspace{0.2cm} \vdots \\[3mm] W_M(\textbf{s}) & = \lambda_{M1} U_1(\textbf{s}) + \lambda_{M2} (\textbf{s}) + \dots + U_M(\textbf{s}). \end{split} \tag{4.2} \end{align}\]

For the application, the main objective of the multivariate disaggregation model is to disaggregate PM2.5, PM10, and ozone by increasing the spatial resolution from \(0.1^\circ\) to \(0.02^\circ\), which corresponds approximately to a change from \(10\) km to \(2\) km. We adopt the LMC structure defined in Equations (4.1) and (4.2), and include elevation as a covariate. The resulting model is

\[\begin{align} \begin{split} \text{pm}_{2.5}(\mathbf{s}) & = \alpha_1+\beta_1 \cdot \text{elevation} (\mathbf{s}) + z_{1}(\mathbf{s}) + e_1(\mathbf{s}) \\ \text{pm}_{10}(\mathbf{s}) & = \alpha_2 +\beta_2 \cdot \text{elevation} (\mathbf{s}) + \lambda_1 z_{1}(\mathbf{s})+z_2(\mathbf{s})+ e_2(\mathbf{s})\\ \text{ozone}(\mathbf{s}) & = \alpha_3 + \beta_3 \cdot \text{elevation} (\mathbf{s}) + \lambda_2 z_{1}(\mathbf{s})+\lambda_3 z_2(\mathbf{s})+z_3(\mathbf{s}) +e_3(\mathbf{s}) \end{split} \tag{4.3} \end{align}\]

where \(\alpha_1\), \(\alpha_2\), and \(\alpha_3\) are intercepts, and \(\beta_1\), \(\beta_2\), and \(\beta_3\) are regression coefficients for elevation for PM2.5, PM10, and ozone, respectively. The terms \(z_1(\mathbf{s})\), \(z_2(\mathbf{s})\), and \(z_3(\mathbf{s})\) are spatially structured independent random effects, modeled as zero mean Gaussian processes with a Matérn covariance function. The terms \(e_1(\mathbf{s})\), \(e_2(\mathbf{s})\), and \(e_3(\mathbf{s})\) represent unstructured errors, modeled as zero mean Gaussian noise that is independent across space.

4.5 Model inputs for INLA

For INLA modeling, in addition to the input data, spatial mesh, and prediction points, we require further components for estimation and prediction. These include the SPDE specification, the projection matrices, and the stacks for fitting and prediction. In this section, we describe how these elements are defined for the INLA implementation.

4.5.1 SPDE espeficication and projection matrix

Here we describe how to define the SPDE model on the triangulated mesh and how to construct the projection matrix. This step is similar to the first part of Section (3.5), but we extend the setup to the multivariate case with three responses. In particular, we define three response objects, \(\texttt{y1}\), \(\texttt{y2}\), and \(\texttt{y3}\), as matrices of dimension \(n_{\mathrm{ar}} \times n_{\mathrm{pp}}\), where \(n_{\mathrm{ar}}\) is the number of observed cells and \(n_{\mathrm{pp}}=3\) is the number of pollutants. Each matrix is filled with \(\texttt{NA}\) values, except for the column corresponding to the pollutant being modeled, which is populated with the observed values. For example, \(\texttt{y1}\) stores PM2.5 in the first column, \(\texttt{y2}\) stores PM10 in the second column, and \(\texttt{y3}\) stores ozone in the third column. This construction matches the multivariate linear predictor used in the stacking and projection steps.

spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh,
                          alpha = 2,
                          constr = TRUE)

n.ar <- nrow(map) # number of initial regions
nv <- mesh$n # number of mesh nodes
n.pp <- 3 # number of response variables

# Projection matrix from initial data to the triangulated mesh
A.m <- matrix(0, n.ar, nv)
inter <- as.list(st_contains(map[,c()],mesh_sf))

for (i in 1:n.ar){
  idx <- inter[[i]]
  A.m[i,idx] <- 1/length(idx)
}
A.m <- as(A.m, "dgCMatrix")

# Projection matrix for prediction locations
A.pr <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = dp)

# First response matrix for PM2.5
y1 <- matrix(NA, nrow = n.ar, ncol = n.pp)
y1[, 1] <- dfm$pm2p5

# Second response matrix for PM10
y2 <- matrix(NA, nrow = n.ar, ncol = n.pp)
y2[, 2] <- dfm$pm10

# Third response matrix for Ozone
y3 <- matrix(NA, nrow = n.ar, ncol = n.pp)
y3[, 3] <- dfm$ozone

4.5.2 Estimation and prediction stacks

Now we create the stack for estimation. In contrast to the univariate case in Section 3.5, the multivariate model requires separate stacks for each response variable. We therefore build three auxiliary stacks, \(\texttt{stk.y1}\), \(\texttt{stk.y2}\), and \(\texttt{stk.y3}\), corresponding to PM2.5, PM10, and ozone, respectively, following the dependence structure in Equation (@ref\tag{4.2}). Each stack specifies the response vector, the projection matrices \(\texttt{A}\) that link observations to the shared and pollutant specific latent fields, and the corresponding fixed effects, including elevation and an intercept. Finally, we combine these auxiliary stacks into a single estimation object, \(\texttt{stk.est.m}\), using \(\texttt{inla.stack(stk.y1, stk.y2, stk.y3)}\).

# Create the stack for y1 (PM2.5)
stk.y1 <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = y1),
  A = list(A.m,A.m,1),
  effects = list(
    intercept.y1 = rep(1, nv),
    spatial.field.sh = 1:nv,
    elev.1 = map$elev/1000 # convert m to km
  ),
  tag = "y1")

# Create the stack for y2 (PM10)
stk.y2 <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = y2),
  A = list(A.m,A.m,A.m,1),
  effects = list(
    intercept.y2 = rep(1, nv),
    sh.copy.y2 = 1:nv,
    spatial.field.y2 = 1:nv,
    elev.2 = map$elev/1000 # convert m to km
  ),
  tag = "y2")

# Create the stack for y3 (Ozone)
stk.y3 <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = y3),
  A = list(A.m,A.m,A.m,A.m,1),
  effects = list(
    intercept.y3 = rep(1, nv),
    sh.copy.y3 = 1:nv,
    y2.copy.y3 = 1:nv,
    spatial.field.y3 = 1:nv,
    elev.3 = map$elev/1000 # convert m to km
  ),
  tag = "y3")

stk.est.m <- inla.stack(stk.y1, stk.y2, stk.y3)

Then we construct the prediction stack on the fine grid. We define three auxiliary prediction stacks, \(\texttt{stk.y1.pred}\), \(\texttt{stk.y2.pred}\), and \(\texttt{stk.y3.pred}\), with responses set to \(\texttt{NA}\) because predictions are required at locations where \(y\) is unobserved. In contrast to the estimation stacks, the projection matrix is now \(\texttt{A.pr}\), which links the prediction locations to the mesh, and elevation is taken from \(\texttt{map_pred}\). We combine the three auxiliary stacks into \(\texttt{stk.pred.m}\), and then merge estimation and prediction into a single object, \(\texttt{stk.full.m}\).

# Stack for predicting PM2.5
stk.y1.pred <- inla.stack(tag = "y1.pred",
                         data = list(y = matrix(NA, nrow=nrow(dp),ncol=n.pp)),
                         A = list(A.pr, A.pr, 1),
                         effects = list(
                           intercept.y1 = rep(1, nv),
                           spatial.field.sh = 1:nv,
                           elev.1 = map_pred$elev/1000 # convert m to km
                         ))

# Stack for predicting PM10
stk.y2.pred <- inla.stack(tag = "y2.pred",
                         data = list(y = matrix(NA, nrow=nrow(dp),ncol=n.pp)),
                         A = list(A.pr, A.pr, A.pr, 1),
                         effects = list(
                           intercept.y2 = rep(1, nv),
                           sh.copy.y2 = 1:nv,
                           spatial.field.y2 = 1:nv,
                           elev.2 = map_pred$elev/1000 # convert m to km
                         ))

# Stack for predicting Ozone
stk.y3.pred <- inla.stack(tag = "y3.pred",
                         data = list(y = matrix(NA, nrow=nrow(dp),ncol=n.pp)),
                         A = list(A.pr, A.pr, A.pr, A.pr, 1),
                         effects = list(
                           intercept.y3 = rep(1, nv),
                           sh.copy.y3 = 1:nv,
                           y2.copy.y3 = 1:nv,
                           spatial.field.y3 = 1:nv,
                           elev.3 = map_pred$elev/1000 # convert m to km
                         ))

# stack for prediction
stk.pred.m <- inla.stack(stk.y1.pred, stk.y2.pred, stk.y3.pred)

# stack for estimation + prediction
stk.full.m <- inla.stack(stk.est.m, stk.pred.m)

4.6 Fitting the multivariate model with INLA

To fit the multivariate model in Equation (4.3), we define the \(\texttt{INLA}\) formula \(\texttt{formMult}\). Compared with the univariate case, the main differences are that we include pollutant specific fixed effects, namely three intercepts, \(\texttt{intercept.y1}\), \(\texttt{intercept.y2}\) and \(\texttt{intercept.y3}\), and three elevation effects, \(\texttt{elev.1}\), \(\texttt{elev.2}\) and \(\texttt{elev.3}\), and we represent cross dependence through shared and copied spatial fields. The term \(\texttt{f(spatial.field.sh, model = spde)}\) defines a shared spatial component, while the clauses \(\texttt{copy = "spatial.field.sh"}\) and \(\texttt{copy = "spatial.field.y2"}\) introduce scaled copies of previously defined fields, with \(\texttt{fixed = FALSE}\) indicating that the scaling parameters are estimated. We then fit the model with \(\texttt{inla()}\) using the combined stack \(\texttt{stk.full}\). Since all three responses are continuous, we set \(\texttt{family = rep("gaussian", 3)}\). Finally, we summarize the fixed effects in a table. For additional details on multivariate modeling in \(\texttt{INLA}\), see (Palmí-Perales, Gómez-Rubio, and Martinez-Beneito 2021).

# Time consuming: This code can  take around 40 minutes to run.
# To monitor progress, uncomment the line `verbose = TRUE` in the `inla()` call.

# INLA formula
formMult <- y ~ 0 + intercept.y1 + intercept.y2 + intercept.y3 +
  elev.1 + elev.2 + elev.3 +
  f(spatial.field.sh, model = spde) +
  f(sh.copy.y2, copy = "spatial.field.sh", fixed = FALSE) +
  f(spatial.field.y2, model = spde) +
  f(sh.copy.y3, copy = "spatial.field.sh", fixed = FALSE) +
  f(y2.copy.y3, copy = "spatial.field.y2", fixed = FALSE) +
  f(spatial.field.y3, model = spde)

# Fitting and prediction
# resM <- inla(
#  formula=formMult,
#  #verbose = TRUE,
#  data = inla.stack.data(stk.full.m, spde = spde),
#  family = rep("gaussian", 3),
#  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stk.full.m),
#                           compute = TRUE, link = 1),
#  control.compute = list(config=TRUE,return.marginals.predictor = TRUE),
# )

#saveRDS(resM, file = "data/models/mult-model-1.rds")
resM <- readRDS("data/models/mult-model-1.rds")

# Summary of the fixed effects of the model
resM$summary.fixed |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Table 4.1: Table 4.2: Posterior summary of the fixed effects (intercept and elevation coefficient) for the multivariate model of PM2.5, PM10 and Ozone concentrations in Portugal.
mean sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant mode kld
intercept.y1 8.345 0.022 8.302 8.345 8.387 8.345 0
intercept.y2 13.399 0.027 13.347 13.399 13.451 13.399 0
intercept.y3 53.480 0.056 53.371 53.480 53.589 53.480 0
elev.1 -0.438 0.073 -0.581 -0.438 -0.295 -0.438 0
elev.2 -0.455 0.090 -0.631 -0.455 -0.279 -0.455 0
elev.3 3.356 0.187 2.988 3.356 3.723 3.356 0

Table (4.1) summarizes the posterior distributions of the fixed effects in the multivariate model. The intercepts represent the baseline mean levels at zero elevation, with posterior means of 8.34~\(\mu\)g/m\(^3\) for PM2.5, 13.4~\(\mu\)g/m\(^3\) for PM10, and 53.48~\(\mu\)g/m\(^3\) for ozone. Elevation shows a negative association with particulate matter, since the posterior credible intervals for \(\texttt{elev.1}\) and \(\texttt{elev.2}\) exclude zero, with posterior means of \(-0.44\) and \(-0.45\), implying decreases of about 0.44 and 0.45~\(\mu\)g/m\(^3\) per 1~km increase in altitude for PM2.5 and PM10, respectively. In contrast, ozone shows a positive association with elevation, with a posterior mean of 3.3 and a credible interval that also excludes zero, indicating an increase of about 3.3~\(\mu\)g/m\(^3\) per 1~km increase in altitude.

4.7 Input data and predicted values for multivariate data

After fitting the model, Figure (4.2) shows the three pollutants together, with PM2.5, PM10, and ozone on the coarse CAMS grid in the first row and the corresponding posterior mean predictions on the finer grid in the second row. As in the univariate case, the finer grid predictions shows more local spatial variation, and the predicted values can span a slightly wider range than the coarse inputs, which helps bring out possible hotspots or cleaner areas that are hidden at 0.1\(^\circ\) resolution. The main added value here is that the three pollutants are modeled jointly, so the predictions also use the spatial dependence between pollutants, allowing the model to borrow information across PM2.5, PM10, and ozone and produce a more coherent multivariate disaggregation.

# get indexes of each response variable
idx.y1 <- inla.stack.index(stk.full.m, 'y1.pred')$data
idx.y2 <- inla.stack.index(stk.full.m, 'y2.pred')$data
idx.y3 <- inla.stack.index(stk.full.m, 'y3.pred')$data

# Input grid
map$pm2p5 <- dfm$pm2p5
map$pm10 <- dfm$pm10
map$ozone <- dfm$ozone

# Prediction
map_pred$pm2p5 <- resM$summary.linear.predictor[idx.y1, "mean"]
map_pred$pm10 <- resM$summary.linear.predictor[idx.y2, "mean"]
map_pred$ozone <- resM$summary.linear.predictor[idx.y3, "mean"]

# Plots
vars <- c("pm2p5", "pm10", "ozone")
labs <- c("PM2.5", "PM10", "Ozone")

plot_list_obs  <- vector("list", length(vars))
plot_list_pred <- vector("list", length(vars))

for (i in seq_along(vars)) {
  plot_list_obs[[i]] <- ggplot(map) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data[[vars[i]]]), color = NA) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(name = labs[i]) +
    geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "black") +
    coord_sf(
      xlim = c(-10, -6),
      ylim = c(36.5, 42.5),
      expand = FALSE
    ) +
    ggtitle(paste("Observed", labs[i])) +
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9),
      plot.margin = margin(t = 5.5, r = 5.5, b = 18, l = 5.5)
    )

  plot_list_pred[[i]] <- ggplot(map_pred) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = .data[[vars[i]]]), color = NA) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(name = labs[i]) +
    geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "black") +
    coord_sf(
      xlim = c(-10, -6),
      ylim = c(36.5, 42.5),
      expand = FALSE
    ) +
    ggtitle(paste("Predicted", labs[i])) +
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9),
      plot.margin = margin(t = 5.5, r = 5.5, b = 18, l = 5.5)
    )
}

p_obs  <- wrap_plots(plot_list_obs,  ncol = 3)
p_pred <- wrap_plots(plot_list_pred, ncol = 3)

p_obs / p_pred

Figure 4.2: Observed and disaggregated pollutant fields over Portugal. The top row shows the observed mean PM2.5, PM10, and ozone on the coarse CAMS grid, and the bottom row shows the corresponding posterior mean predictions from the multivariate disaggregation model on the finer grid. Country boundaries are overlaid for reference.

5 Spatio-temporal disaggregation of Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) in India

In this section, we extend the univariate spatial disaggregation framework to a spatio-temporal setting using Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) at 550 nm over India. The goal is to increase the spatial resolution from \(0.75^\circ\) to \(0.25^\circ\), which corresponds approximately to 84 km and 28 km near the equator, and to refine the temporal resolution from 3-hourly to hourly. We use AOD data from the Atmospheric Composition Reanalysis 4 (EAC4) produced by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) (Inness, Ades, Agustí-Panareda, et al. 2019). This reanalysis is available from 2003 and is provided on a global \(0.75^\circ \times 0.75^\circ\) grid at 3-hour time steps. In contrast to the purely spatial case, the disaggregation is carried out jointly in space and time, so we can produce estimates both at finer spatial locations and at intermediate hourly time points that are not available in the original product. As in the previous examples, we include altitude as a covariate to help explain spatial variation in the AOD field.

5.1 Data acquisition and preprocessing

To download Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) data from EAC4, we follow the same ADS setup described earlier, but under the “ERA-Interim Product licence”. In this example we focus on the first day of January 2024, which is why we request the AOD variable at 550 nm for the period \(\texttt{date = ["2024-01-01/2024-01-05"]}\). We use the dataset identifier \(\texttt{"cams-global-reanalysis-eac4"}\), and the argument \(\texttt{variable = ["total_aerosol_optical_depth_550nm"]}\) selects total AOD at 550 nm. The argument \(\texttt{time}\) specifies the available 3 hour time stamps from \(\texttt{"00:00"}\) to \(\texttt{"21:00"}\), and \(\texttt{data_format = "grib"}\) downloads the data in GRIB format. GRIB (GRIdded Binary) is a compact binary format widely used in meteorology and reanalysis products to store gridded fields efficiently, especially for large spatio temporal datasets.

As mentioned above, the original dataset is provided in GRIB format. To read these files in R, we use terra. We first load the GRIB file as a raster object and then reshape it into a long format, which is more convenient for preprocessing and for constructing the spatio-temporal model. Table (5.1) shows the first six rows of the resulting dataset for AOD at the global scale. If you have problems downloading or processing the data, we recommend skipping this step and going directly to the next chunk of code.

# Time consuming: This code can  take around 2 minutes to run
# read GRIB file
r <- rast("data/AOD-data-day.grib")

# create clean layer names from the time dimension
tt <- time(r)

names(r) <- paste0("t", seq_len(nlyr(r)))

# convert to dataframe in wide format
df_init <- as.data.frame(r, xy = TRUE, na.rm = FALSE)

# reshape to long format
df_long <- reshape(
  df_init,
  varying = names(r),
  v.names = "value",
  timevar = "layer",
  times = seq_len(nlyr(r)),
  direction = "long"
)

# add datetime, date, and hour
df_long$datetime <- tt[df_long$layer]
df_long$date <- as.Date(df_long$datetime)
df_long$hour <- as.integer(format(df_long$datetime, "%H"))

# rename coordinates
names(df_long)[names(df_long) == "x"] <- "longitude"
names(df_long)[names(df_long) == "y"] <- "latitude"

# keep only what you want
df_long <- df_long[, c("date", "hour", "longitude", "latitude", "value")]

# sort values by latitude and longitude
df_long <- df_long[order(df_long$date, df_long$hour, df_long$latitude, df_long$longitude), ]
row.names(df_long) <- NULL

head(df_long) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 8) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Table 5.1: Table 5.2: First six rows of the long format dataset obtained from the GRIB AOD file, showing date, hour, longitude, latitude, and AOD (550 nm) values after reshaping and sorting.
date hour longitude latitude value
2024-01-01 0 -180.00 -90 0.00581898
2024-01-01 0 -179.25 -90 0.00581898
2024-01-01 0 -178.50 -90 0.00581898
2024-01-01 0 -177.75 -90 0.00581898
2024-01-01 0 -177.00 -90 0.00581898
2024-01-01 0 -176.25 -90 0.00581898

After converting the dataset to long format, we filter it to the study region of interest, India. Figure (5.1) shows the spatial distribution of AOD over India for the first day of January 2024, giving a first look at the main spatial patterns and areas with higher aerosol load. The object \(\texttt{sq_st}\) defines the spatial domain used in this study. In spatio-temporal modeling, keeping a very large region increases the number of spatial locations and, as a result, the model becomes more computationally demanding and takes longer to fit. For this reason, we also provide, as commented code, a smaller domain that can be used to reduce computational cost. A comparison of fitting and prediction times for the larger and smaller domains is discussed in Section (5.6). Finally, to avoid working with the full global dataset, we provide the filtered long format dataset for India as \(\texttt{data-st.csv}\).

# Define the squared study region and convert to dataframe
sq_st <- ext(64.875, 90.375, 5.625, 33.375) # big
# sq_st <- ext(67.875, 90.375, 14.625, 30.375) # small

# Coment this if you had problems downloading or prepocesing the dataset
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# Filtering and saving the dataset
df_st <- df_long[
  (df_long$longitude >= sq_st$xmin) &
  (df_long$longitude <= sq_st$xmax) &
  (df_long$latitude  >= sq_st$ymin) &
  (df_long$latitude  <= sq_st$ymax),]
write.csv(df_st, "data/data-st.csv", row.names = FALSE)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------

# Read the filtered dataset
df_st <- read.csv("data/data-st.csv")

# Make an index for each different date and hour
df_st$time <- match(
  paste(df_st$date, df_st$hour),
  unique(paste(df_st$date, df_st$hour))
)
df_st$hour_lab <- sprintf("%02d:00", df_st$hour)

# Download India boundary
boundary_india <- ne_countries(scale="medium", returnclass="sf") |>
  subset(admin %in% c("India","Pakistan")) |>
  st_transform(4326)

# Plot
ggplot(df_st, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, fill = value)) +
  geom_raster() +
  geom_sf(data = boundary_india, fill = NA, color = "black",
          inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ hour_lab, ncol = 4) +
  coord_sf(
    xlim = range(df_st$longitude),
    ylim = range(df_st$latitude),
    expand = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(
    title = "AOD on First of January of 2024",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude",
    fill = "AOD"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )

Figure 5.1: Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) values over the study region in India on January 1, 2024, at 3-hour intervals from 00:00 to 21:00 UTC. Each panel shows the spatial distribution of AOD on the original grid, with the boundary of India overlaid in black.

5.2 Input grid, spatial mesh, and prediction locations

In this section, we specify the spatio temporal mesh and other elements used for disaggregation. We reuse the spatial triangulated mesh from the univariate case in Section (3.2) and introduce a one dimensional temporal mesh over the study period. We also define the input spatial grid and the spatio temporal prediction locations used to obtain estimates at the finer resolution. Figure (5.2) summarizes these elements. The first panel shows a portion of the triangulated spatial mesh, represented by black segments, together with the coarse input grid, shown in red. The second panel shows the spatial prediction locations, shown as blue points, defined within each coarse grid cell. The third panel shows the temporal mesh as a sequence of knots along the time axis, red dots are the observations and black dots are the mesh points. To achieve the spatial disaggregation from \(0.75^\circ\) to \(0.25^\circ\), we define prediction locations within each coarse cell using the spatial factor \(\texttt{spf_st}=3\), which increases the number of locations per cell by a factor of \(3 \times 3 = 9\). To refine the temporal resolution from 3 hourly to hourly, we use the temporal factor \(\texttt{tf}=3\), which introduces intermediate time points between the original observations.

# Initial squared grid
map_st <- st_as_sf(st_make_grid(sq_st, n = c(length(unique(df_st$longitude)),
                               length(unique(df_st$latitude)))))
st_geometry(map_st) <- "geometry"
st_crs(map_st) <- "EPSG:4326"

# Spatial mesh

# convert the square in a sf object
sq_st_sf <- st_as_sf(as.polygons(sq_st))

# Create equally space points for the emsh
hexpts_st <- fm_hexagon_lattice(
  bnd = st_buffer(sq_st_sf, 1),
  edge_len = 0.5
)

# Create the mesh based in the previous points
smesh <- fm_mesh_2d(
  loc = hexpts_st,
  max.edge = 1,
  offset = 0.5
)

# Create the temporal mesh
tf <- 3 # temporal factor
nt <- tf * max(df_st$time)
tmesh <- inla.mesh.1d(
  loc = seq(from=1,to=nt,by =1))

# Spatial mesh as a sf object
smesh_sf <- st_as_sf(data.frame(x=smesh$loc[,1],y=smesh$loc[,2],id=1:smesh$n),
                    coords = c("x","y"),crs="EPSG:4326")

# prediction points
spf_st <- 3 # spatial factor for spatio temporal modeling
def <- abs(unique(df_st$latitude)[2]-unique(df_st$latitude)[1])/2

x <- seq(min(df_st$longitude) - def*((spf_st-1)/spf_st),
         max(df_st$longitude) + def*((spf_st-1)/spf_st),
         length.out = length(unique(df_st$longitude))*spf_st)

y <- seq(min(df_st$latitude) - def*((spf_st-1)/spf_st),
         max(df_st$latitude) + def*((spf_st-1)/spf_st),
         length.out = length(unique(df_st$latitude))*spf_st)

dp_st <- as.matrix(expand.grid(x, y))

dpdf_st <- data.frame(
  x = rep(dp_st[, 1], times = nt),
  y = rep(dp_st[, 2], times = nt),
  time = rep(seq_len(nt), each = nrow(dp_st))
)

dpdf_st_sf <- st_as_sf(dpdf_st,coords = c("x","y"),crs="EPSG:4326")
dpdf_st_sf$id <- 1:nrow(dpdf_st)

# Plots
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), pty = "s")
plot(smesh,xlim = c(66,71),ylim = c(13,18)) # xlim = c(63,68),ylim = c(4.5,9.5)
plot(map_st$geometry, add = TRUE, border = "red", lwd = 2)

plot(map_st$geometry, border = "red", lwd = 2,xlim = c(67,71),ylim = c(14,18)) # xlim = c(64,67.5),ylim = c(5.5,7.5)
plot(dpdf_st_sf$geometry, add = TRUE, col = "blue", lwd = 1)

plot(tmesh$loc[1:6], rep(0, 6), pch = 16, cex = 1.5,
     xaxt = "n",yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "", ylab = "", bty = "n",
     col = c("black", "red", "black", "black", "red", "black"))
lines(range(tmesh$loc[1:6]), c(0, 0), col = "gray")

Figure 5.2: Spatio temporal discretization for AOD disaggregation. Left, triangulated spatial mesh (black) overlaid with the coarse input grid (red). Middle, spatial prediction locations (blue) defined within each coarse cell for $ exttt{spf_st}=3$. Right, one dimensional temporal mesh, red dots observation points, black dots mesh points.

5.3 Covariates

We incorporate elevation as a covariate using the SRTM30\(+\) Version \(11\) land surface digital elevation model (DEM), produced by the Scripps Institution of Oceanography (SIO), which provides global land elevation at approximately \(1\)~km resolution on a regular latitude longitude grid . Elevation is included to relate AOD variability to topography and to improve the explanatory power of the spatio temporal disaggregation model over India. We obtain the elevation data through the ERDDAP API by submitting a query that downloads only the spatial window covering the study region. In R, we use the package curl to download the resulting NetCDF file, which is then read as a raster with terra. To use this covariate within our framework, we align its support with both the original AOD grid and the finer prediction grid by extracting mean elevation values for the input cells at \(0.75^\circ\) resolution and for the prediction locations at \(0.25^\circ\) resolution. Figure (5.3) illustrates elevation over India on the input grid, shown on the left, and on the prediction grid, shown on the right, with country boundaries for reference.

# Time consuming: This code takes 1 minute to be executed
# Dowloading the elevation for India
# url <- paste0(
#   "https://pae-paha.pacioos.hawaii.edu/erddap/griddap/",
#   "srtm30plus_v11_land.nc?",
#   "elev[(", sq_st$ymin-1, "):1:(", sq_st$ymax+1, ")]",
#   "[(", sq_st$xmin-1, "):1:(", sq_st$xmax+1, ")]"
# )
# curl_download(
#   url,
#   destfile = "data/srtm30plus_india.nc",
