5.4 Model

In this model, spatio-temporal disaggregation is used to increase resolution in both dimensions, from \(0.75^\circ\) to \(0.25^\circ\) in space and from 3h to 1h in time. For this, we use INLA together with INLAspacetime to model a latent field that depends on space and time with a non separable covariance structure. In particular, we assume the existence of a latent continuous spatio-temporal process for AOD, defined on a triangulated spatial mesh and a temporal mesh, but observed only at aggregated space-time locations. The observations are linked to the latent field through a spatio-temporal extension of the aggregation operator used in the spatial case, as defined in Equation ((??)).

\[\begin{equation} \text{AOD}(\mathbf{s},t) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{elevation}(\mathbf{s}) + z(\mathbf{s},t) + e(\mathbf{s},t) \tag{5.1} \end{equation}\]

where \(\beta_0\) is the intercept and \(\beta_1\) is the regression coefficient for elevation. The component \(z(\mathbf{s},t)\) captures the structured spatio-temporal variation in AOD, and it is modeled as a zero mean Gaussian process with a non separable covariance structure given by the solution of the SPDE in Equation ((??)). The term \(e(\mathbf{s},t)\) represents unstructured error term, modeled as zero mean Gaussian noise that is independent across space and time.

5.5 Model inputs for INLA

As in the previous applications, INLA modeling requires a few additional objects beyond the ones we have already defined, namely the input data, the spatial mesh, the temporal mesh, and the prediction points. In this section, we describe the remaining components needed for fitting and prediction. These are the SPDE specification, which in this case is spatio-temporal, the projection matrices that link observations and prediction locations to the latent field, and the stacks used for model fitting and prediction.

5.5.1 SPDE espeficication and projection matrix

Here we describe how to define the SPDE model on the spatio-temporal mesh and how to construct the projection matrices that link the data to the mesh and the mesh to the prediction points. This is an extension of the spatial setup in Section (3.5) to the spatio-temporal setting. We build the spatio-temporal SPDE using r pkg(“INLAspacetime”), taking the spatial and temporal meshes defined previously as inputs. We use \(\texttt{model = "121"}\), which corresponds to a non separable model with parameters \((\alpha_t,\alpha_s,\alpha_e)=(1,2,1)\) (Lindgren et al. 2023).

For the spatio-temporal projection matrix, we construct the spatial and temporal components separately. The spatial part is built in the same way as in Section (3.5). For the temporal part, we create a matrix where rows correspond to the original 3-hour observation times and columns correspond to the finer hourly time points, and we use Equation ((??)) to distribute each observation over the corresponding disaggregation times. We then obtain the full spatio-temporal projection matrix by taking the Kronecker product of the spatial and temporal projection matrices. We repeat the same idea to build the projection matrix for the prediction points. Overall, these matrices provide the link from the input observations to the spatio-temporal mesh, and from the mesh to the prediction locations.

# SPDE definition
stmodel <- stModel.define(
  smesh = smesh,
  tmesh = tmesh,
  model = "121",
  control.priors = list(
    prs = c(2, 0.05),
    prt = c(100, 0.05),
    psigma = c(2, 0.05)))

n.ar <- nrow(map_st) # number of initial regions
nvs <- smesh$n # number of spatial mesh nodes

# Spatial projection matrix
A.ms <- matrix(0, n.ar, nvs)
inter <- as.list(st_contains(map_st[,c()],smesh_sf))

for (i in 1:n.ar){
  idx <- inter[[i]]
  A.ms[i,idx] <- 1/length(idx)
}
A.ms <- as(A.ms, "dgCMatrix")

# Temporal projection matrix from input to mesh
A.t <- matrix(0, nrow = nt / tf, ncol = nt)
A.t[cbind(rep(1:(nt / tf), each = tf), 1:nt)] <- 1 / tf

# Temporal projection matirx from mesh to predictions
A.t.pred <- diag(1, nt)

# Projection matrix for spatio temporal input data
A.st <- as(kronecker(A.t, A.ms), "dgCMatrix")

# Projection matrix for prediction locations
A.pr.s <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = smesh, loc = dp_st)
A.pr.st <- as(kronecker(A.t.pred, A.pr.s), "dgCMatrix")

Finally, we define the stacks for estimation and prediction. Since elevation is treated as time-invariant, we replicate its values across the temporal dimension so that the covariate matches the length of the spatio-temporal latent field. We do this for both the input grid, using \(\texttt{elev_map_st}\), and the prediction grid, using \(\texttt{elev_pred_st}\), converting elevation from meters to kilometers by dividing by \(1000\).

The estimation stack, \(\texttt{stk.est.st}\), combines the observed AOD values \(\texttt{df_st\$value}\) with the spatio-temporal projection matrix \(\texttt{A.st}\), and includes an intercept, the spatio-temporal index \(\texttt{st}\), and the replicated elevation covariate. The prediction stack, \(\texttt{stk.pred.st}\), has the same structure but uses \(\texttt{NA}\) in the response to request predictions at the spatio-temporal prediction locations through \(\texttt{A.pr.st}\). Compared with the multivariate case, this setup follows the same idea as the spatial univariate example and is more straightforward. Finally, we combine both stacks into \(\texttt{stk.full.st}\), which is used for fitting and prediction in the \(\texttt{INLA}\) call.

# Covariate in the spatio-temporal setting
elev_map_st <- rep(map_st$elev/1000,(nt/tf)) #/1000 to convert km to m
elev_pred_st <- rep(map_pred_st$elev/1000,nt) #/1000 to convert km to m

# Stack for estimation AOD
stk.est.st <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = df_st$value),
  A = list(A.st,1),
  effects = list(list(
    intercept = rep(1,(nt*nvs)),
    st = 1:(nt*nvs)),
    elev = elev_map_st
    ),
  tag = "y")

# Stack for predicting AOD
stk.pred.st <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = rep(NA, nrow(dpdf_st))),
  A = list(A.pr.st,1),
  effects = list(list(
    intercept = rep(1, (nt*nvs)),
    st = 1:(nt*nvs)),
    elev = elev_pred_st),
  tag = "y.pred")

# Stack for estimation and prediction
stk.full.st <- inla.stack(stk.est.st, stk.pred.st)

5.6 Fitting the spatio-temporal disaggregation model with INLA

To fit the spatio temporal disaggregation model in Equation (5.1), we define the \(\texttt{INLA}\) formula \(\texttt{form_st}\). This is similar to the spatial case, but the latent field is now indexed in space and time. The term \(\texttt{0 + intercept}\) adds an explicit intercept, \(\texttt{elev}\) includes elevation as a covariate, and \(\texttt{f(st, model = stmodel)}\) defines the spatio-temporal latent field through \(\texttt{stmodel}\). We fit the model with \(\texttt{inla()}\) using the full stack \(\texttt{stk.full.st}\), and \(\texttt{control.predictor}\) supplies the projection matrix needed to compute fitted values and predictions.

Since this model can take a long time to fit, especially for the larger spatial domain, we use a practical strategy based on \(\texttt{theta.ini}\). Here \(\texttt{theta.ini}\) provides initial values for the latent field hyperparameters and the fixed effects, and we pass them through \(\texttt{control.mode}\) and \(\texttt{control.fixed}\). In practice, giving reasonable initial values helps the optimizer converge faster and reduces total runtime. In our experiments, fitting the model without \(\texttt{theta.ini}\) took about \(6\) h \(19\) min for the big region and about \(2\) h for the small region. Using \(\texttt{theta.ini}\) reduced the runtime to about \(1\) h \(19\) min for the big region and about \(27\) min for the small region. We provide two sets of starting values, one for the smaller domain and one for the larger domain, and you can switch between them by selecting the corresponding \(\texttt{theta.ini}\) line in the code.

form_st <- y ~ 0  + intercept + elev +f(st, model = stmodel)

#theta.ini <- c(10.8,1.96, 7.2,-0.51,0.83,-0.13) # small
theta.ini <- c(11.3,2.06, 7.49,-0.64,0.61,-0.11) # big

# Summary of the fixed effects of the model
res_st$summary.fixed |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Table 5.3: Table 5.4: Posterior summary of the fixed effects (intercept and elevation) for the spatio-temporal model of AOD at 550nm in India.
mean sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant mode kld
intercept 0.611 0.252 0.116 0.611 1.105 0.611 0
elev -0.115 0.014 -0.143 -0.115 -0.087 -0.115 0

Table (5.3) summarizes the posterior distributions of the fixed effects in the spatio-temporal model. AOD is a unitless measure related to aerosol load in the atmosphere. The posterior mean of the intercept is 0.611, which can be interpreted as the baseline mean AOD at zero elevation. Elevation shows a negative association with AOD, with a posterior mean of \(-0.115\) and a credible interval that excludes zero, implying a decrease of about 0.115 in AOD per 1~km increase in altitude.

5.7 Input data and predicted values for spatio temporal modeling

After fitting the model, Figure (5.4) summarizes the spatio-temporal disaggregation results for the first hours of January 1, 2024. The first column shows the observed AOD on the original coarse resolution at 00:00, 03:00, and 06:00. The remaining columns show the posterior mean predictions on the finer spatio-temporal grid, providing hourly maps from 00:00 to 08:00. The disaggregated fields add spatial detail and can show a slightly wider range than the coarse observations, which helps reveal localized areas with higher or lower aerosol load that may be hidden at the original resolution. In time, the model fills the gaps between the 3-hour observations in a smooth way, producing intermediate hourly maps that remain consistent with the observed patterns while avoiding abrupt changes between time steps.

idx.y <- inla.stack.index(stk.full.st, 'y.pred')$data
dpdf_st$pred <- res_st$summary.linear.predictor[idx.y, "mean"]

dpdf_st$hour_lab <- sprintf("%02d:00", dpdf_st$time-1)

# Download India boundary
boundary_india <- ne_countries(scale="medium", returnclass="sf") |>
  subset(admin %in% c("India","Pakistan")) |>
  st_transform(4326)

# Plot

# Common scale
lim_fill <- range(c(df_st$value, dpdf_st$pred), na.rm = TRUE)

p1 <- ggplot(df_st[df_st$time < 4, ], aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, fill = value)) +
  geom_raster() +
  geom_sf(data = boundary_india, fill = NA, color = "black", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ hour_lab, ncol = 1) +
  coord_sf(
    xlim = range(df_st$longitude),
    ylim = range(df_st$latitude),
    expand = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = lim_fill) +
  labs(
    title = "Observed",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude",
    fill = "AOD"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )

p2 <- ggplot(dpdf_st[dpdf_st$time <= 9, ], aes(x = x, y = y, fill = pred)) +
  geom_raster() +
  geom_sf(data = boundary_india, fill = NA, color = "black", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ hour_lab, ncol = 3) +
  coord_sf(
    xlim = range(df_st$longitude),
    ylim = range(df_st$latitude),
    expand = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = lim_fill) +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude",
    fill = "AOD"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )

(p1 + p2) +
  plot_layout(widths = c(1, 3), guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "right")
